reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent, dual-sourced claims about the storm's devastation, the dramatic mine rescue, and the policy aftermath.
story: In the dry summer of 1910, the newly established U.S. Forest Service faced thousands of small wildfires raging across the Northern Rockies. Then, on August 20, the nightmare began. Hurricane-force winds slammed into the mountains, whipping the scattered blazes into a single, three-million-acre monster. The firestorm incinerated entire towns in minutes, sending flaming trees flying through the air like spears. Darkness fell by midday as a colossal smoke shroud blanked the nation, blinding ships hundreds of miles out in the Pacific. Trapped in the inferno, Forest Ranger Ed Pulaski made a desperate gamble, leading 45 panicked firefighters into an abandoned mine tunnel. Holding them at gunpoint to prevent them from fleeing into the flames, Pulaski held a wet blanket over the entrance until he collapsed. All but five survived. The tragedy claimed at least 85 lives and sparked a century of controversial total fire suppression.
angle: To save his crew from the three-million-acre firestorm, Ranger Ed Pulaski forced his men into an abandoned mine tunnel at gunpoint; his heroic stand saved 40 lives and inspired the famous firefighting tool used today.

claims.claim: The Great Fire of 1910 is also commonly known as the Big Blowup or the Big Burn.
The wildfire burned over three million acres across northern Idaho and western Montana in August 1910.
On August 20, 1910, hurricane-force winds whipped hundreds of smaller fires into a massive, unified firestorm.
The U.S. Forest Service was only five years old in 1910 and was highly unprepared with limited equipment and experience.
President William Howard Taft authorized U.S. Army troops, including the all-black Buffalo Soldiers, to help battle the fires.
Smoke from the fires was so thick that ships 500 miles out in the Pacific Ocean could not navigate by the stars.
Smoke from the massive firestorm traveled as far east as New York.
Roughly one-third of the town of Wallace, Idaho, was completely burned to the ground.
Several towns, including Grand Forks, Taft, De Borgia, Haugan, and Henderson, were completely destroyed by the fire.
A crew of 28 firefighters perished when they were overcome by flames at Setzer Creek near Avery, Idaho.
Forest Ranger Edward Pulaski led a crew of 45 firefighters to shelter in an abandoned mine tunnel near Wallace, Idaho.
Pulaski drew his gun to prevent panicked crew members from leaving the safety of the mine tunnel.
Pulaski held wet blankets over the tunnel entrance to block the flames until he collapsed from smoke inhalation.
Of the 45 men Pulaski led into the mine, 40 survived the disaster.
At least 78 firefighters lost their lives trying to control the massive wildfire.
Following the fire, Edward Pulaski invented the Pulaski tool, an axe-and-hoe combination still used by wildland firefighters today.
The fire was finally extinguished on August 21-22 when a cold front brought rain and early snow.
The catastrophe prompted the U.S. Forest Service to adopt a strict policy of total fire suppression.

disputed: The exact total death toll of the fire is disputed among sources, ranging between 85, 86, and 87. The script should state that between 85 and 87 people died.

The claim that Pulaski drew his gun to prevent his men from fleeing is disputed because it relies primarily on his own later account. The script should attribute this detail with "according to Pulaski" or "as the story goes".
The exact location where the 28-man crew perished is named as Setzer Creek in S1 and S7, but Storm Creek in S6. The script should use Setzer Creek or omit the specific creek's name.
